blocks.text: The builder and results described 61 as an unconditional requirement to win confidence.
61 is labeled an absolute seat majority and a planning target. An initial confidence vote depends on votes for and against, with abstention distinguished from opposition.

A seat-majority target is useful coalition arithmetic but cannot replace the applicable confidence rules. The 2021 government was confirmed 60–59. The same wording correction applies on Results and the homepage.
automated, Oct 5, 2026
The results preparation text said votes for lists below the threshold are shared out.
Votes for a list below the threshold are not transferred. Seats are allocated among lists that passed.
The previous wording could imply that a failed list's votes move to other parties. This correction aligns the preparation and count text with the seat-allocation explanation.
automated, Oct 5, 2026
Alternate prime minister

A post created by a 2020 amendment to Basic Law: The Government for rotation governments. The 2020 law set up the Alternate Prime Minister's Office, to be held by Benny Gantz for 18 months and then passed to Netanyahu, so that the outgoing prime minister could keep the title after vacating the post. The Supreme Court declined to strike the law down.
Annexation

Applying Israeli law and administration to West Bank land. The Knesset has not passed it into law. On Oct 22, 2025, a bill applying Israeli law to "all areas of settlement" passed a preliminary reading 25–24 and was sent to the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee. Supporters call it applying sovereignty; this site says annexation.
Area C

The roughly 60% of the West Bank under full Israeli control under the 1995 Oslo II agreement. In Area A (about 18%) the Palestinian Authority has full control; in Area B (about 22%) the Authority has civil control and Israel security control.
Areas A and B

The two other zones of the 1995 Oslo II division of the West Bank (see Area C). The accords required Israel to transfer certain powers in Areas A and B to Palestinian authorities; the International Court of Justice found in 2024 that the transfers "have remained limited and partial" and that Israel "has retained significant control in relation to security matters."
Ashkenazi

Jews whose families trace their roots mainly to central and eastern Europe; plural Ashkenazim. Pew found that "fully two-thirds of Ashkenazim identify as secular (Hiloni) Jews," compared with 32% of Sephardim and Mizrahim.
Attorney general

Israel's attorney general heads the criminal prosecution, represents the state and the public interest in court, and gives legal counsel to the government "as the authorized interpreter of the law." Proposals to split the role have been debated for years. The government tried to remove the incumbent attorney general, but Supreme Court rulings halted the dismissal proceedings.
Bader–Ofer method

Israel's rule for sharing out leftover seats, adopted with the Bader–Ofer Law of 1973, one of whose goals was "to strengthen the larger parties." After whole seats are handed out, each leftover seat goes to the list with the most votes per seat it would then hold, one seat at a time.
Ballot letters

Each list runs under a short code of Hebrew letters printed on its ballot slip, and the Central Elections Committee reports the count by those letters, not by party name. In 2022 the Likud column in the committee's results file was headed מחל.
Ballot slip

Israelis vote on paper. Behind a screen, the voter takes one printed slip for the chosen list, seals it in an envelope and drops the envelope in the ballot box. A slip with writing on it, a torn slip, or an envelope holding more than one slip is disqualified.
Basic Laws

Israel has no single written constitution. The assembly elected to write one turned itself into the Knesset and chose instead "an incremental constitution, made up of a series of 'basic laws' to be legislated over the years." Basic Law: The Knesset and Basic Law: The Government set the rules for elections and for forming governments.
Bedouin

The State Comptroller counted around 325,000 Bedouin in the Negev at the end of 2023, about 20% of the region's population. It estimates the "dispersed Bedouin population," which includes the unrecognized villages, at 70,000 to 90,000.
Bibi

Benjamin Netanyahu's nickname since childhood. In July 2019 he passed David Ben-Gurion as Israel's longest-serving prime minister, at 4,876 days; he was first in office from 1996 to 1999 and again from 2009.
The bloc

Parties backing Benjamin Netanyahu for prime minister. In 2022, the blocs' vote totals were "almost identical," but his camp won "a clear majority of 64 seats." This site groups lists as the Netanyahu bloc, the Anti-Netanyahu bloc (Zionist parties), lists between the blocs, and the Joint List and Ra'am. These polling groups do not imply a coalition agreement.
Central Elections Committee

The body that runs Knesset elections. It is headed by a Supreme Court justice chosen by the court's justices, currently Deputy President Noam Sohlberg, and its plenum, 31 members for the outgoing Knesset, is made up of representatives of the Knesset's factions. It can disqualify a list or candidate on grounds set in law, including incitement to racism.
Chief Rabbinate

The state religious authority for Jews, led by two chief rabbis, one Ashkenazi and one Sephardi, elected for 10-year terms by a body of 150. It oversees kashrut certification, marriage, divorce and more, and the chief rabbis alternate at the head of the Chief Rabbinate Council and the Supreme Rabbinical Court.
Coalition

The parties that together hold the government. No single party has ever won a majority of Knesset seats, so every Israeli government has been a coalition, of between three and nine factions. Governments formed after elections have almost always had the support of at least 61 members.
Coalition agreement
The signed deal between the factions forming a government, specifying which ministries each faction will head and the guiding principles and policies the government will promote.
Constructive no-confidence

Israel's rule for toppling a sitting government: a no-confidence motion passes only if 61 Knesset members support an alternative government, naming its prime minister, other ministers and basic guidelines. IDI calls the mechanism "among the most rigid in the world."
Consultations

After the election, the president holds consultations with the representatives of the factions elected to the Knesset, then nominates one of their leaders to form a government. The nominee has 28 days to do so, which can be extended by 14.
Dati leumi

National-religious Jews, also called Religious Zionists: Orthodox in practice and fully part of the Zionist state, including army service. In the Central Bureau of Statistics' 2026 survey, 12.4% of Jewish adults called themselves "religious" (dati), the official category closest to this group. Not the same as the party Religious Zionism.
Development towns

In the words of the Times of Israel, "around 30 development towns created in the 1950s and 1960s mainly in the north and south of Israel, primarily to house immigrants from North Africa." Sderot, Netivot, Ofakim, Dimona, Beit She'an and Kiryat Shmona are among them.
Dissolution

The Knesset can end its term early by passing a dissolution law, which needs at least 61 votes on the third reading. It is also dissolved automatically if the state budget is not passed on time (in normal years, by March 31). Either way, a new election follows.
Double-envelope votes

Ballots cast anywhere other than the voter's assigned polling station, officially in "outer envelopes." Most come from members of the security forces stationed far from home; others from hospital patients and staff, prisoners and detainees, diplomats posted abroad, residents of senior-citizen facilities and persons with disabilities.
Druze

A religious community whose tradition, in Pew's words, "incorporates elements of Islam, Hinduism and even classical Greek philosophy." In Israel they are about 2% of the population, concentrated in the north. Unlike most Muslim and Christian citizens, Druze men serve in the army: about six in ten told Pew they had served (45%) or were serving (15%).
East Jerusalem

The part of Jerusalem Israel captured in 1967, to which it applied its law, jurisdiction and administration; a 1980 Basic Law proclaimed "complete and united Jerusalem" its capital. The UN Security Council and the International Court of Justice treat it as occupied territory. Israel, the court noted, "regards Palestinians residing there as foreigners" and requires residence permits.
Electoral threshold

A list needs at least 3.25% of the valid votes to win any seats, the rule since the 2015 election. In 2022 that meant 154,855 votes. Votes for lists that fall short are dropped before seats are handed out.
Exit poll

The estimates broadcast by Israel's three main television channels, Kan, Channel 12 and Channel 13, the moment polls close at 10:00 p.m. They are projections of seats per list, not a count, and can differ from the final result.
Gaza disengagement

Israel's 2005 withdrawal from the Gaza Strip, in which more than 8,000 Israelis were removed from 21 settlements, including the Gush Katif communities. The territory was handed over to the Palestinian Authority before Hamas seized it in 2007.
Green Line
The 1949 ceasefire line separating Israel and the West Bank, the boundary in place before the 1967 war. In 2022 Tel Aviv began marking it on its classroom maps, against Education Ministry practice.
Hamas

Islamist Palestinian movement, rival of Fatah, Mahmoud Abbas's party. It won the 2006 Palestinian legislative elections, took control of Gaza "in a violent coup against Fatah in 2007" and has ruled it since. The Times of Israel calls it a terror group. It led the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel (see the timeline).
Haredi draft

The fight over conscripting Haredi men, who for most of the state's history could defer service while studying full-time in yeshiva. In June 2024 a unanimous nine-justice Supreme Court panel found "no legal basis for avoiding the recruitment of yeshiva students." Israeli debate calls men who do not report "draft evaders"; this site says yeshiva students who did not report.
Haredim

Israel's most strictly religious Jews (singular Haredi), often called ultra-Orthodox in English. In Central Bureau of Statistics figures for 2025, released in September 2026, 11.5% of Jewish adults called themselves Haredi.
Hezbollah

A Shiite Muslim political party and militant group based in Lebanon, backed by Iran, with seats in Lebanon's parliament since 1992. After the Hamas-led attack of October 2023 it began firing rockets, mortars and drones across the border. An Israeli campaign in 2024 considerably weakened it, and the two sides agreed to a U.S.-brokered ceasefire in November 2024.
High Court of Justice

The name for Israel's Supreme Court when it hears petitions against government action. The court serves as both a superior court of appeals and a first-instance administrative court, so citizens and groups can challenge the government directly before it. English coverage often says "the High Court"; this site says Supreme Court.
Hiloni

A secular Jew; plural hilonim. In the Central Bureau of Statistics' newest count, 39.6% of Jews aged 20 and over called themselves secular, the largest single group but not a majority. The rest: 21.8% traditional, not so religious; 14.0% traditional-religious; 12.4% religious; 11.5% Haredi.
Intifada

The name for the Palestinian uprisings against Israeli occupation. The first began in December 1987 and ran until the 1993 Oslo Accords; by Al Jazeera's count "more than 100 Israelis were killed by Palestinians" and "at least 1,000 Palestinians were killed by Israeli forces." The second began in September 2000 (see the timeline).
Iron Dome

Israel's mobile system for intercepting short-range rockets and artillery, at ranges of up to 70 km. Development began in 2007 and the first units were deployed in 2011. From fiscal 2011 to 2015 the United States provided "almost $1.3B" for its batteries, interceptors, co-production and maintenance.
Judea and Samaria

The biblical name for the West Bank: Judea is the southern part, Samaria the northern. It is the main name in internal Israeli discourse, while the territory is known internationally as the West Bank. In 2018 the US ambassador, David Friedman, sought to use it in official statements. This site says West Bank.
Judicial overhaul

The plan Justice Minister Yariv Levin announced in January 2023 to bar courts from using a "reasonableness" test on government decisions, give the government a built-in majority on the committee that picks judges, curb judicial review of laws, let 61 Knesset members re-enact a law the court struck down, and let ministers appoint their own legal advisers.
Judicial Selection Committee

The nine-member panel that appoints judges, with political representatives of the coalition and opposition, three Supreme Court justices and two Israel Bar Association representatives. A law passed on March 27, 2025, which takes effect only in the next Knesset, replaces the bar's seats with lawyers chosen by the coalition and opposition and removes the judges' influence over Supreme Court picks.
Knesset
Israel's parliament, made up of 120 members (MKs), with no second chamber. Elections are due every four years, but from 1996 to 2022 they came on average every 2.4 years.
Law of Return

The 1950 law, amended in 1970, that grants citizenship to anyone with at least one Jewish grandparent. The Chief Rabbinate recognizes as Jews only those with a Jewish mother or an Orthodox conversion it approves, so many immigrants admitted under the law are not Jewish in the Rabbinate's eyes and cannot marry in a state-sanctioned wedding.
Left and right

In Israel, left and right are defined mostly by positions on the Palestinians, the occupied territories and a Palestinian state. Economic views are a separate, weaker dimension: an expert survey of party positions places Shas and United Torah Judaism on the right on the Palestinian question and on the left on economics.
List

What Israelis vote for: a party or alliance's ranked slate of candidates. Voters cannot change the order, and the ballot itself does not even carry candidates' names, except sometimes the list leader's. A list's seats go to the names at the top of its slate, in order.
Mandate

The task of forming a government, which the president gives to one Knesset member after the election. The law sets no rule for choosing. The president typically picks the leader of the largest party, "but this is by no means mandatory"; what counts is who seems best placed to win the Knesset's confidence.
Mandate (seat)
In Israeli polls and election coverage, a "mandate" often simply means a Knesset seat, as in a party "expected to come second with 19 mandates."
Masorti

Traditional Jews, plural masortim, who sit between secular and religious on the scale Israeli surveys use. The Central Bureau of Statistics splits them into those "traditional but not particularly religious" (21.8% of Jews aged 20 and over) and "traditional-religious" (14%). Not the same as Mizrahi.
Military rule

Israel's rule over Palestinians in the West Bank through its army since 1967. The International Court of Justice found in 2024 that Israel "has to a large degree substituted its military law for the local law": Palestinians are tried in military courts, settlers in Israeli civilian courts. Since late 2022 a civilian minister in the Defense Ministry decides civil affairs in Area C.
Mizrahi

Jews whose families came from the Middle East and North Africa; plural Mizrahim. In IDI's May 2025 survey, 35.2% of Jewish adults described themselves as Mizrahi, 39.8% Ashkenazi and 15.3% mixed. Not the same as masorti, which describes religious practice rather than origin.
Nakba

"Catastrophe": Palestinians' name for their mass displacement in 1947–49. By the first half of 1949, "at least 750,000 Palestinians in total were forcibly expelled or fled outside of their homeland," Al Jazeera reports. Palestinians mark it every year on May 15.
Nation-State Law

Basic Law: Israel – The Nation State of the Jewish People, passed 62–55 in July 2018. In the Times of Israel's translation it declares that "the right to exercise national self-determination in the State of Israel is unique to the Jewish people" and that "the Arabic language has a special status in the state."
Occupied

This site's word for the West Bank and the parts of Gaza Israel holds. The International Court of Justice's non-binding 2024 advisory opinion refers to "the Palestinian territory occupied since 1967." Netanyahu answered: "The Jewish people are not occupiers in their own land."
Opposition
The parties in the Knesset that are not part of the government. It is led by the Leader of the Opposition, usually from the largest opposition faction, a post with special powers and status.
Oslo Accords

The agreements between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization signed on September 13, 1993, by Yitzhak Rabin and Yasser Arafat, which created the Palestinian Authority. They set a five-year interim period of Palestinian self-government and postponed issues such as Jerusalem and refugees. Oslo II, in 1995, divided the West Bank into Areas A, B and C.
Outpost
A West Bank settlement without official status. Peace Now defines outposts as "settlements established by governments of Israel since the 1990s in an unofficial and illegal manner."
Outside support

Backing a government in Knesset votes without joining its cabinet or holding ministries. After Shas left Rabin's coalition in September 1993, its 56 MKs relied on outside support from Arab factions. Ra'am joined the Bennett–Lapid coalition in 2021. The Builder separates cabinet membership, hypothetical outside support and abstention; these choices do not imply an agreement.
Palestinian Authority

The Palestinian self-government created under the Oslo Accords as a "supposedly temporary" body; it "administers limited rule" over Areas A and B of the West Bank. A final treaty was due within five years and has not been reached.
Palestinian citizens of Israel

This site's term for Arab Muslims, among them the Negev Bedouin, and Arab Christians who hold Israeli citizenship. IDI and other sources say "Arab citizens of Israel" or "Arabs." IDI counted 1,595,300 Arab citizens outside East Jerusalem at the end of 2020, 17.2% of the population, a figure that includes Druze.
President

Israel's head of state, elected by the Knesset for a seven-year term by an absolute majority (61 members) in a secret ballot. The role is mostly ceremonial, but the president gives the task of forming a government to a Knesset member after an election, signs laws, and grants pardons.
Reasonableness standard

A doctrine under which courts could void government and ministerial decisions they found unreasonable. The Knesset curbed it in July 2023, the second overhaul-era law to pass after a March 2023 change limiting when a prime minister can be removed as incapacitated. On January 1, 2024, a full 15-justice Supreme Court panel struck that law down 8–7.
Religious Zionism (party)

A party led by Bezalel Smotrich. For 2026, Smotrich and Zehut leader Moshe Feiglin agreed to run together in a "technical bloc," which they said was meant "to prevent loss of votes." The party is distinct from the national-religious movement (dati leumi) whose name it shares.
Rotation government

A government with two heads, a prime minister and an alternate, who switch posts on a date set in advance. The form was created in 2020 for the Netanyahu–Gantz government, whose ministers were split into two blocs, one tied to each leader, each head holding a veto over important decisions by the other.
Settlement

In Peace Now's definition, one of the Jewish communities "that Israel established after 1967 beyond the Green Line on land occupied in the Six-Day War." Some 30% of settlers are Haredi and live in cities built for them, such as Modi'in Illit and Beitar Illit.
Sovereignty

The word supporters of annexation use: "applying sovereignty" means extending Israeli law to West Bank land. When the cabinet expanded Israeli control over West Bank land in February 2026, Bezalel Smotrich called it part of "the normalization and de facto sovereignty revolution that we are leading"; the Foreign Ministry called it "an administrative measure." This site says annexation.
Status quo

The arrangement on religion and state that goes back to David Ben-Gurion's 1947 letter to the Haredi party Agudat Yisrael, which promised that the new state would take Jewish religious concerns into account on Shabbat, kashrut and matrimonial law. The letter had no legal force, but "the status quo" is still the name for the arrangements that followed.
Surplus-vote agreement

A pre-election pact between two lists, also called a vote-sharing agreement. When leftover seats are handed out, the pair are treated as a single list, which raises their chance of an extra seat. Only two lists can sign together, and the agreement counts only if both pass the threshold.
Torato Umanuto

Hebrew for "his Torah is his trade": the arrangement, set up after the state was founded, under which yeshiva students could claim that "Torah [study] is my occupation" and receive a deferral of military service. The deferrals expired on June 30, 2023.
Transitional government

The common name, not found in legislation, for an outgoing government that keeps serving until a new government is formed. The law sets no limit on its powers, to avoid a "governance vacuum," but transitional governments have a narrower "scope of reasonableness" and must act with restraint.
West Bank

The territory west of the Jordan River that Israel captured in the 1967 war and has held under military occupation since (see Occupied). This site's name for it; internal Israeli discourse refers to it primarily by its biblical name, Judea and Samaria.

blocks.text: Should Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) yeshiva students be drafted into the army?
Most Israeli Jews are conscripted at 18. Haredi men in full-time religious study have largely been exempt since 1948, and the Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that the exemption has no legal basis.
No one should be compelled to serve
Exempt those who study Torah full time
Draft only those who leave yeshiva
Raise Haredi service step by step
Everyone serves, in the army or a civilian service
Should power shift from the courts to the Knesset and the government?
Israel has no written constitution. Its Supreme Court can strike down laws and government decisions, and the 2023 judicial overhaul, which set out to curb it, brought months of mass protest.
Yes, curb the Supreme Court's powers
Let the Knesset override the court in limited cases
Settle the balance in a Basic Law, a kind of constitution
No, keep the courts independent
Who should investigate the failures of October 7?

Israel's 1968 law sets up a state commission of inquiry whose members are chosen by the president of the Supreme Court. The government has proposed a different commission whose members the court would not choose.
A commission set up outside the 1968 law
An independent inquiry; the exact form can wait
A state commission of inquiry under the 1968 law
Should Israel annex land in the occupied West Bank?
Israel has held the West Bank since 1967 without annexing it. About half a million Israeli settlers and some three million Palestinians live there. Annexation would apply Israeli law to the land.
Annex the whole West Bank
Annex Area C or chosen areas
Back sovereignty in principle, but not by law now
Expand settlements without annexing
Separate from the Palestinians
No annexation; work toward a Palestinian state
Should there be a Palestinian state?
A Palestinian state beside Israel has been the aim of most international peace plans since the 1990s. Most lists running in 2026 oppose one; a few support it.
No, oppose a Palestinian state
Not now; it is not on the agenda
Separation as part of a regional deal
Yes, support a Palestinian state
Who should run marriage, conversion and the rules for Shabbat?

Israel has no civil marriage: Jews marry through the Orthodox Chief Rabbinate, and many couples marry abroad instead. The rabbinate also controls conversion, and Shabbat rules such as public transport are set nationally.
Keep them in Orthodox hands
Allow civil marriage, and let towns set Shabbat rules
Allow civil marriage and recognise non-Orthodox conversion
What should economic policy put first?
The cost of living is among Israelis' top worries. The lists' economic priorities can coexist rather than run from one end to another, so the match here is on the priority you put first.
Free markets and a smaller state
Lower living costs and narrower gaps
Rewarding those who serve in the army or reserves
Budgets for communities that have been left behind
Should young Haredi men who have left yeshiva be required to serve?
Even some lists that defend the exemption for full-time students disagree over men who are no longer studying.
Yes, require them to serve
No compulsory service
In a service framework, military or civilian, who should be exempt?
The draft plans differ most on who would still be exempt.
No one: no exemptions or quotas
A small number of outstanding scholars
Everyone studying in yeshiva full time
Should the 2025 law that gave politicians more say in choosing judges be repealed?

The March 2025 law replaced the Israel Bar Association's two seats on the committee that selects judges with public representatives chosen by the coalition and the opposition. It takes effect in the next Knesset.
Repeal and replace it
Keep it
Should the Knesset be able to pass again a law the Supreme Court has struck down?
An "override clause" was the most contested part of the 2023 overhaul. The answers differ on how large a majority it would need.
Yes, with a simple majority of 61
No override
Only with a special majority, 70 MKs or more
Should the courts keep "reasonableness" as grounds to overturn government decisions?
In 2023 the Knesset abolished the standard for decisions by the cabinet and ministers; the Supreme Court struck that law down in 2024.
Keep it, but narrow it
Abolish it for decisions by the cabinet and ministers
Should couples be able to marry in a civil ceremony inside Israel?
Today a civil marriage performed abroad is registered in Israel, but none can be performed in the country.
Yes, allow a civil option
No, keep marriage religious
Should towns be able to run public transport on Shabbat?
Most buses and trains stop from Friday evening to Saturday evening. A few cities run limited services of their own.
Yes, let each town decide
No, keep the current Shabbat rules
Should Israel recognise conversions to Judaism done outside the Orthodox establishment?
Recognition decides who is Jewish under Israeli law for marriage and burial, which matters to many Reform and Conservative Jews.
Yes, extend recognition
No, keep Orthodox authority
Who has a vote?

Knesset elections choose a national legislature. Citizenship, residency and location are different questions: people affected by Israeli decisions do not all have a vote in this election. Begin with the citizenship and residency distinctions.
Read who votes
Does living under the effects of a government's decisions automatically give someone a Knesset vote?
Yes, every resident has the same national voting rights
No; eligibility depends on citizenship and other legal conditions
National and municipal eligibility differ. The guide distinguishes citizens, East Jerusalem permanent residents and Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza.
Votes become 120 seats

Voters choose a ranked electoral list in one nationwide constituency. A list needs 3.25% of valid votes to receive seats. Votes for a list below the threshold are not transferred to another list; seats are allocated among the lists that pass.
See how votes become seats
What happens to votes cast for a list below the threshold?
They are transferred to its closest ally
They produce no seats for that list
The threshold applies to valid votes. Passing lists share the seats; surplus-vote agreements operate between eligible passing lists, not as a rescue for a failed list.
A party is not a bloc

An electoral list can contain several parties. A bloc is a grouping used to describe possible alliances; it is not a single ballot choice. Read two profiles, then compare the same parties on one concrete question.
Explore the parties
If two lists belong to the same bloc, do they necessarily share every policy?
Yes; a bloc is one party with one platform
No; cooperation can coexist with policy differences
Blocs describe groupings, not complete agreement. Compare recorded positions and missing evidence before describing a shared agenda.
Who can form a government?

The largest list does not automatically govern. It needs a governing arrangement and Knesset confidence. An absolute seat majority is 61 of 120; that planning target does not by itself establish how a confidence vote will go or whether parties will cooperate.
Try a governing arrangement
Does winning the largest number of seats guarantee that a list forms the government?
Yes; the largest list automatically governs
No; it still needs an arrangement that can win confidence
Seat arithmetic, recorded commitments and policy cooperation are separate questions. The formation guide explains the legal process; the builder helps you explore the arithmetic and constraints.
Compare one real question

Choose two or more lists in Compare. Find one shared recorded position and one difference. Open the evidence: what was said, when, and what remains unknown? A category count is not a forecast of governing stability.
Compare recorded positions
What can missing evidence establish?
That parties agree because no disagreement is recorded
That the evidence is incomplete
Silence is not agreement. Look for complete dated evidence and distinguish a shared objective from agreement on how to achieve it.
I have five minutes
The essential distinctions, with one tool to try.
Read the polls with these distinctions in mind
Help me understand the parties
From ballot choices to recorded disagreements and governing arrangements.
Read an issue in depth
Israeli citizen
Living in Israel, including Palestinian and Druze citizens
Eligible from 18
Eligible from 17
Subject to the relevant voter register. Religion and ethnicity do not create different citizenship-based voting rights.
Israeli permanent resident, without citizenship
For example, many Palestinians in East Jerusalem; check each person's actual status
Not eligible
Eligible from 17
Municipal voting requires residence and registration in the relevant local authority. Naturalization changes the national-vote position.
Golan resident: citizenship must be checked
Druze communities in the Israeli-annexed Golan Heights
Citizen: eligible from 18; noncitizen: not eligible
Permanent residents: eligible from 17
Being Druze or living in the Golan does not establish whether a person has Israeli citizenship. Local voter-register conditions apply.
Israeli citizen in a West Bank settlement
The occupied West Bank
Eligible from 18
Check local council rules
Citizens can vote in Knesset elections from settlement polling places. Local council arrangements should not be inferred from the national rule.
Palestinian resident without Israeli citizenship or permanent residency
The West Bank or Gaza
Not eligible
No Israeli municipal right on that basis
Place of residence alone does not confer Israeli voting rights. Palestinian elections are a separate system, described below.
Israeli citizen abroad
Outside Israel on election day
Check registration and voting location
Check residence and the local register
There is no general overseas absentee vote. Most registered voters must return to vote; limited official overseas categories have special arrangements.
